options: The two seats have different expected returns (first-move advantage), so a global baseline credits the seat instead of the moves
A global baseline has higher variance only for single-player games
REINFORCE cannot use any baseline in multi-agent settings
The global baseline makes the game no longer zero-sum
explain: If the first player wins more often, a global baseline makes nearly every first-player move look good and every second-player move look bad. RAE subtracts a separate running mean per game and seat, so only better-than-usual play for that seat is reinforced.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Provider prompt caching is a different thing from semantic caching
question: You add the user's name and the current time to the very top of the system prompt to personalize replies. What happens to the two caches?
options: Prompt caching stops working because the prefix now differs per request; the semantic cache is unaffected if it embeds only the user's question
Both stop working
Neither is affected
The semantic cache stops working; prompt caching is unaffected
explain: Prefix matching is exact from the first token, so a per-request value at the top breaks every reuse. Put stable content first and variable content last. A semantic cache keyed on the user's question does not see the system prompt, which is exactly why it needs scoping when the system prompt matters.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: IMDSv2: session tokens, PUT and a hop limit of 1
question: An attacker has remote code execution on an EC2 instance that requires IMDSv2 with a hop limit of 1. Can they read the role credentials?
options: No: the token requirement blocks them
No: the TTL of 1 drops the token
Only if the instance has a public IP address
Yes: code on the instance can send its own PUT, receive the token directly and use it
explain: IMDSv2 protects against requests relayed by something else (WAFs, proxies, SSRF, routers). Code running on the instance is exactly the legitimate client IMDS is built to serve. That is why role permissions must still follow least privilege.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Insecure deserialization: when loading data runs code
question: A Java service checks `if (!(obj instanceof Cart)) throw ...` right after `readObject()`. Why does this not stop a gadget chain?
options: instanceof is slow
The chain runs inside readObject, while the object graph is being built, before the check executes
Gadget chains only affect PHP
Cart must implement Externalizable
explain: Deserialization hooks run as each object is reconstructed. By the time readObject returns and your check runs, any side effect has already happened. Filters must act before construction, which is what ObjectInputFilter does.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Path traversal and safe path joins
question: What is the strongest design for a "download your invoice" endpoint?
options: Accept a file name and strip every dot and slash
Accept an invoice ID, check the user owns it, look up the stored path server-side, and never put user text in a path
Accept a full path but only allow paths ending in .pdf
Accept a file name and URL-decode it twice before checking
explain: If user input never reaches the filesystem API, there is nothing to traverse, and the ownership check also closes the IDOR hole from the access-control course. Extension checks and character stripping are both known to be bypassable.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: LM programs: why the runtime should see the whole program
question: Why does the interpreter send the shared prefix to the runtime before the fork branches?
options: So that the prefix is computed and inserted into the radix tree once; branches arriving together would otherwise each find nothing cached and each prefill it
Because the runtime cannot accept prompts longer than the prefix
To let the runtime pick a different model for each branch
Because RadixAttention only works when requests arrive one at a time
explain: If both branches arrive at the same moment with nothing cached, each matches zero tokens and each computes the shared part. The paper calls the fix a frontend hint: it simplifies runtime matching and is one of the co-design benefits in its ablation.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Structured output today: grammar masks inside the SGLang scheduler
question: Your application needs an EBNF grammar for a small domain-specific language. Which `--grammar-backend` cannot serve it?
options: xgrammar
outlines
llguidance
None of them: SGLang supports only JSON schema
explain: The docs list EBNF support for XGrammar and llguidance; Outlines in SGLang supports JSON schema and regex only.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Dijkstra's algorithm: settle nodes in order of distance
question: A teammate stops Dijkstra as soon as T is first inserted into the queue, to save time. Using the toy run, why is this a bug in general?
options: It is not a bug; the first label any node receives is final
It only matters when the graph has negative weights
Insertion happens after settling, so the check never fires
Tentative labels can still drop after insertion, as C did (7 from S, then 6 via D)
explain: A label is only final when its node is popped as the queue minimum. C first got 7 directly from S and later improved to 6 through D. The same can happen to t, so the stop test must be on the pop, not the push.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Real engines: turn costs, live traffic and time-dependent travel
question: Why does an edge-based (arc-based) graph make turn costs routable with an unchanged Dijkstra?
options: It deletes all intersections, so turns no longer exist
It stores turn costs in the heuristic
It merges parallel roads into one vertex
Its vertices are road segments, so a turn is an ordinary weighted arc between two segments
explain: Once a state is the road you are on, the cost of turning from it onto the next road is just an arc weight, and plain Dijkstra applies. The price is a larger graph: 28 directed segments instead of 9 junctions in the toy.

courseTitle: Signal processing basics: sampling, the FFT and filters
lessonTitle: IIR filters, zero-phase filtering and real sensor data
question: A 20 s recording at 50 Hz shows a spectral peak at 1.5 Hz. The bins are 0.05 Hz apart. A colleague wants 0.01 Hz precision on the rate. What is the honest way to get finer frequency resolution?
options: Record a longer segment (100 s gives 0.01 Hz bins)
Raise the sampling rate to 250 Hz
Zero-pad to 5000 samples, which gives true 0.01 Hz resolution
Use a causal Butterworth filter before the FFT
explain: Resolution is 1/duration, so 0.01 Hz needs about 100 s of data. A higher fs only extends the frequency range. Zero-padding interpolates between bins (useful to locate a single clean peak more precisely) but does not separate close frequencies, as Smith points out.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Masks instead of branches: compares, blends and AVX-512
question: Your AVX2 select gives out[i] = 2x for x = NaN lanes on one machine and 0 on another build. Which part of the code is the likely suspect?
options: The blendv argument order
The compare predicate (ordered versus unordered)
movemask
loadu versus load
explain: An ordered predicate like _CMP_GT_OQ returns false when an input is NaN, so NaN lanes become 0; an unordered predicate such as _CMP_NLE_UQ (not less-or-equal) returns true for NaN. If two builds use different predicates or a compiler rewrites the comparison under -ffast-math, NaN handling changes.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: Bump allocation: a bounds check and a pointer add
question: A server bump-allocates parsed headers into a per-request arena and resets it when the response is sent. A cache stores a pointer to one parsed header so later requests can reuse it. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, because resetting the arena only moves a pointer and does not change the bytes
Memory leaks, because the header is never freed
The cached pointer dangles: after reset the next request bump-allocates over the same bytes
The arena must be locked, because a bump pointer cannot be reset while other pointers exist
explain: Reset makes the whole chunk free again, and the very next request reuses those addresses. The cached pointer now aliases unrelated data. Objects that outlive the phase must be copied out (or allocated elsewhere).

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Three modules, one loop: how slime is laid out
question: A colleague changes `--hf-checkpoint` to point at the latest exported checkpoint every time they resume training, "so SGLang starts from the right weights". Is this needed?
options: Yes, otherwise SGLang samples from the original weights for the whole run
Only for MoE models
No: train.py syncs the Megatron weights into SGLang before the first rollout
No, because SGLang reads Megatron's torch_dist checkpoint directly
explain: The usage guide says slime synchronizes parameters from Megatron to SGLang before the first training step, so the HF checkpoint initializes SGLang (architecture, tokenizer, initial tensors) rather than carrying trained weights. Its config still matters for quantized rollout (lesson 4). SGLang does not read torch_dist checkpoints.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: The trainer side: from scored samples to a policy-gradient step
question: A run uses `--advantage-estimator grpo --kl-coef 0.05`, hoping to keep the policy near the reference. The reference model loads and slime computes a per-token KL, yet training behaves exactly like a run without KL. Why?
options: The KL is computed against the wrong checkpoint
--kl-coef is ignored unless --colocate is set
The coefficient is too small to matter
--kl-coef only shapes rewards for ppo and REINFORCE++; GRPO's advantages ignore it. Use --use-kl-loss --kl-loss-coef instead
explain: compute_advantages_and_returns computes the KL whenever kl_coef is non-zero, but get_grpo_returns copies only the reward to every token. GRPO's KL term goes into the loss, and slime asserts that kl_coef and kl_loss_coef are not both set.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: What a blockchain is: a shared ledger that nobody owns
question: In the toy chain, an attacker edits block 0 and also recomputes block 0's digest. What does the checker report?
options: Every block is ok, because block 0's digest is correct again
Block 1 is broken, because it still stores the old digest of block 0
Only block 2 is broken
Nothing can be checked once a digest changes
explain: Block 1 stores the previous digest e7a83d, but block 0 now hashes to b3efbf. The attacker would have to rewrite block 1, then block 2, and so on to the tip.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: A toy chain in Python, and thinking in invariants
question: In the toy chain, a function moves 3 ETH to Bo and then raises Revert. What does Bo end up with?
options: The 3 ETH, because the transfer completed before the error
Half, as a partial refund
It depends on whether Bo is a contract
Nothing extra: the revert restores the balances saved when the call began
explain: Calls are atomic: the snapshot taken at the start of the call is restored. The EVM behaves the same way, which is also what makes flash loans possible (lesson 10).

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Price oracles, spot prices and flash loans
question: A lending protocol values collateral with the spot price of a deep AMM pool. A reviewer says the pool is too deep to manipulate. What is wrong with that argument?
options: Deep pools cannot be manipulated at all, so nothing
AMMs have no spot price
Only TWAP oracles can be flash-loaned
Flash loans supply enormous capital for one transaction, so depth raises the cost but does not remove the attack
explain: Depth sets how much capital a price move needs; flash loans make that capital free for one transaction. The attack works whenever the profit exceeds fees and slippage.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Bridges: where many of the largest DeFi thefts happened
question: Which change most directly prevents the Nomad failure?
options: Raising gas limits
Adding more validators
Rejecting the zero root explicitly, so a default value can never be a trusted one
Moving to proof of stake
explain: The bug was that an unset value equalled a trusted value. Explicitly refusing the zero root (and testing upgrades against 'unproven message' cases) closes it whatever the validator setup.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Incident response on chain, and where to practise
question: Why does monitoring the bridge's invariant matter even after the bug is already being exploited?
options: It reverses the stolen transactions
It identifies the attacker's real name
It is required for an audit
Many exploits repeat over many transactions or blocks (Nomad's copycats); detecting the first one and pausing stops the rest
explain: On-chain theft is often spread over many transactions. Fast detection plus a pause turns a total loss into a partial one, as the toy run shows (60 versus 10).

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Enrichment: asset, identity and intel context, and where it lies
question: Enrichment says the source IP of a failed-login burst is "malicious (feed-A, last seen 2 years ago)" and geolocates to a mobile carrier. What is the soundest reading?
options: Confirmed attacker; block the IP everywhere
Weak evidence: the intel is old and carrier IPs are shared by many subscribers, so judge the alert on the login pattern itself
Definitely benign, because carrier IPs are always legitimate users
Ignore the alert, since enrichment disagrees with itself
explain: Both enrichment facts are weak: stale reputation, and an address that many unrelated customers share. Blocking it could cut off your own mobile users (collateral damage, in RFC 6269's words). The behaviour in the logs is better evidence than the label.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Cloud key misuse, and what Snowflake customers could see in 2024
question: GuardDuty raises InstanceCredentialExfiltration.OutsideAWS for a web server's role credentials. The source IP is the company's own on-premises VPN gateway, and the web team confirms the server routes outbound traffic through it. What is the right outcome?
options: Benign true positive: document it and add a suppression rule scoped to that finding type and the gateway's IP range
True positive: rotate everything and escalate
False positive: disable GuardDuty
Ignore it; GuardDuty will learn the behaviour anyway
explain: This is the benign case AWS describes, and AWS recommends exactly a two-criteria suppression rule. Letting the model learn it silently is worse: you lose the record of why, and anything later using that same remote address, including a real attacker behind the gateway, would stop producing findings.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Talking to users, owners and leaders during an investigation
question: You suspect an employee is copying customer data to a personal cloud account. Who do you contact first?
options: The employee, to hear their side
Their manager, by email
The incident lead and, through them, HR and legal, keeping the case need-to-know
The whole security team channel
explain: Possible insider cases are sensitive: contacting the employee or a wide channel can tip them off, harm an innocent person, or break legal process. The NCSC advises segregating insider threat work for exactly these reasons.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Why Johnny can't encrypt: usability is a security property
question: In the study, seven participants encrypted messages to their team with their own public key. What kind of failure was this?
options: A bug in PGP's encryption code
Participants were not motivated to finish the task
The team members' email software was misconfigured
A mismatch between the user's mental model of keys and how public-key encryption works, with no feedback showing the error
explain: PGP encrypted exactly as asked. The users misunderstood whose key to use, and the interface gave no warning until the team replied that they could not read the message.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Anatomy of a pretext: how manipulation is built and broken
question: An attacker offers employees free 'priority IT support' if they install a remote access tool. Which form in NIST's list is this?
options: Thread-jacking
Quid pro quo
Tailgating
Baiting
explain: Quid pro quo offers a service or favour in return for an action. Baiting leaves an object as a lure; thread-jacking hijacks an existing email conversation; tailgating is physical.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: SIM swaps, bribed insiders and people you do not employ
question: The CSRB found Lapsus$ paid insiders at telecom providers. Why is that hard to counter with technical controls alone?
options: The insider uses legitimate access, so the action looks like normal work
Insiders always use encrypted messages
Telecom systems have no logs
Bribes are legal in some countries
explain: An insider approving an MFA request or doing a SIM swap is using tools they are allowed to use. Least privilege, strong customer authentication before sensitive actions, and reporting channels matter more than filters.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Dropped USB drives, implants and unattended screens
question: A keyboard-class USB device appears on a finance PC at 02:00 while the screen is locked and no one badged into the floor. What should the SOC conclude first?
options: The user bought a new keyboard
Device control is working
Nothing, as the screen is locked
A possible physical intrusion with a hardware addition; isolate the host and check badge logs and CCTV
explain: The combination of time, locked screen and no badge entry points to someone physically present who should not be. A locked screen does not stop a device from being plugged in or a network implant from working.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Why single neurons are hard to read: superposition
question: In the pentagon model, which input is decoded wrongly with b = -0.309?
options: Only f1 on
f1 and f2 on (neighbours)
f1 and f3 on (non-neighbours)
No feature on
explain: Non-neighbours have cosine -0.809, so their sum cancels most of each one's own signal (0.191 each) while the shared neighbour f2 gets 0.618. After the bias only f2 survives. Neighbours reinforce each other instead.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Reading a latent: activating examples, logit effects, autointerp
question: An explanation scores 0.95 on simulation using only top-activating excerpts, but 0.30 when the excerpts are sampled across the whole activation range. What is the best reading?
options: The explanation fits the strongest activations but not the weaker ones that make up most firings; it is too narrow
The latent is dead
The simulator model is broken; trust the 0.95
The latent must be monosemantic because 0.95 is high
explain: Top examples can make a latent look cleaner than it is. Towards Monosemanticity and Paulo et al. sample across activation intervals precisely because weaker activations often follow a broader or different pattern.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Build it yourself: train a TopK SAE on GPT-2, then use a released one
question: Your SAE has FVU 0.19 and loss recovered 97.9% (zero ablation) at this residual site. Which extra number best tells you whether it is good enough to splice into the model for an analysis?
options: Its L0, because sparser is always better
The number of latents
Delta LM loss in nats (here about 0.2), compared with what your analysis can tolerate
The decoder norms
explain: Zero-ablating the residual stream is so destructive that loss recovered looks excellent for almost any SAE. Delta LM loss says directly how much worse the spliced model predicts text; 0.2 nats is a large degradation.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Kriging is Gaussian process regression in map coordinates
question: A data scientist fits a GP to sensor data with an RBF kernel plus a white noise kernel. In kriging vocabulary, the white noise variance corresponds to:
options: The range
The sill
The nugget
The Lagrange multiplier
explain: A white noise term adds variance only on the diagonal, exactly like a nugget: semivariance jumps from 0 to the nugget as soon as two points are distinct.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Speculative sampling: guesses that keep the target's distribution
question: Which pair of models has the higher acceptance rate beta for a single position?
options: Both are equal because both drafts put most mass on the first token
explain: beta = sum of min(p, q). First pair: 0.5 + 0.1 = 0.6. Second pair: 0.5 + 0.4 = 0.9. What matters is overlap with the target, not agreeing on the top token.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: EAGLE drafts and prompt lookup decoding
question: Medusa's typical acceptance, Medusa-2, EAGLE-2 and prompt lookup: which of these can change the output distribution compared to the original target model?
options: Only EAGLE-2
Typical acceptance and Medusa-2
Prompt lookup, because copied tokens skip the target
All four
explain: Typical acceptance replaces rejection sampling with a threshold, and Medusa-2 fine-tunes the backbone itself. EAGLE-2 and prompt lookup only change how drafts are proposed; verification with the standard rule keeps the target's distribution.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Whisper: a transformer over 30-second spectrogram windows
question: You pass 12 s of audio to Whisper. What does the encoder process?
options: A 80 x 1200 spectrogram, 600 positions
A 80 x 3000 spectrogram, 1500 positions, with the last 18 s padded with zeros
Three 4 s chunks processed in parallel
The raw 192,000 samples directly
explain: Whisper always feeds the encoder 30 s: the low-level API pads the audio to 480,000 samples, and `transcribe` pads each log-mel window to 3000 frames, so the shape is always 80 x 3000 and the stem always yields 1500 positions. The padded tail is silence, which matters later when we look at hallucinations.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: The map of a process: segments, /proc/PID/maps and ASLR
question: A machine runs with `kernel.randomize_va_space = 1`. Across runs of a PIE program, which region keeps the same position relative to the program's own data segment?
options: The [heap], because heap randomization is only added at setting 2
The [stack]
Shared libraries such as libc
The [vdso]
explain: Setting 1 randomizes the mmap base, the stack and the vdso (so libraries move too) and the PIE code start; the data segment moves with the code. Only setting 2 adds heap randomization, so at 1 the heap starts right where bss ends, run after run.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: Page faults: lazy allocation, copy-on-write and overcommit
question: A 10 GiB Redis-like process (an in-memory key-value database) calls fork to write a snapshot while it keeps serving writes. Memory use climbs sharply during the snapshot. Why?
options: fork copies all 10 GiB up front
The child process leaks heap memory
Every page the parent writes while the child holds the old version triggers a copy-on-write fault and a new private copy
Copy-on-write is disabled for anonymous memory
explain: fork only duplicates page tables. But each page the parent modifies during the snapshot must be copied so the child still sees the old data, so memory grows with the number of distinct pages written. Huge pages make this worse: one small write can copy 2 MiB.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Difference of means: building a vector from contrast pairs
question: In the toy example, the single-pair direction from pair 4 still classifies all eight activations correctly. Why prefer the mean difference anyway?
options: It is the only direction with unit length
It makes projections of negatives exactly zero
Single-pair vectors cannot be added to the residual stream
It is closer to the true concept direction (cosine 0.991 vs 0.891), so steering along it changes less of everything else
explain: Classification only needs the right sign. Steering adds the whole vector, including its off-concept components. Pair 4's direction has a larger share of noise, so adding it would also push unrelated dimensions. The averaged vector is cleaner.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Lab: build, sweep and evaluate a steering vector on a small chat model
question: In the lab, c = +4 gave 0.805 and c = +8 gave 0.633 on test. Which conclusion is right?
options: The vector encodes the opposite behavior
Larger coefficients always help, so the test set must be mislabeled
Past some strength the added vector dominates the stream and disrupts the model, so the response curve turns over; choose c on validation and inspect side effects
Layer 14 was the wrong layer
explain: The steering direction is right (the curve is monotonic from -4 to +4), but at 8 times the vector (norm 8.6 against a stream of about 19) the push disrupts the model and answers drift back toward chance. ITI reports the same inverted U, and CAA saw large multipliers degrade open-ended text.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Ingest: MQTT at the edge, a Kafka log in the middle
question: Sensors publish at QoS 1. Your rollup job sums energy readings per minute and the totals are occasionally slightly too high. Most likely cause?
options: QoS 1 can lose messages, and losses push sums up
QoS 1 retries after a lost PUBACK, so a reading can be delivered twice and counted twice
Kafka reorders records within a partition
MQTT always runs over UDP, which duplicates packets
explain: At least once means no loss but possible duplicates. A sum counts a duplicate twice. The fix is to deduplicate on a reading id (device id plus sequence number) or to write results idempotently (so that writing the same result twice leaves the same outcome as writing it once), covered in the last lesson.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Why recurrence was the bottleneck for sequence models
question: Per Table 1 of the paper, for which sequences is one self-attention layer cheaper in total work than one recurrent layer?
options: Always, because it has O(1) sequential operations
When the sequence length n is larger than the model width d
When n is smaller than d, which is typical for sentence-length inputs
Never; it is only faster because of parallelism
explain: Self-attention costs about $n^2 d$ and a recurrent layer about $n d^2$, so attention does less total work when $n < d$. The paper notes this is most often the case for sentence representations in machine translation (the base model has d = 512). Sequential operations are a separate column: they measure parallelism, not total work.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Positional encoding and the full encoder-decoder stack
question: Which sub-layer holds the most parameters in one base-model encoder layer?
options: Multi-head self-attention, because it has 8 heads
LayerNorm, because it has a gain and bias per dimension
The position-wise feed-forward network, about twice as many as attention
They are equal by design
explain: Attention: 4 x 512^2, about 1.05 million. FFN: 2 x 512 x 2048, about 2.10 million. LayerNorm has only 2 x 512 = 1,024 per instance. Heads split the attention width; they do not add parameters.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Training recipe, quadratic cost and what changed since 2017
question: Which statement about the paper's learning-rate schedule is correct?
options: It starts at its maximum and decays linearly to zero
It is constant at 1e-3 because Adam adapts the rate per parameter
It increases linearly for 4000 steps, then decays with the inverse square root of the step
It increases for the whole run
explain: Equation 3 is the minimum of a linear ramp and an inverse square root curve; the two meet at step = warmup = 4000, where the rate peaks at about 0.70e-3 for d_model = 512.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: BM25 in Lucene and Elasticsearch: fields, tuning, limits
question: You index product records with a 5-word title and a 300-word description, and you want a match in the title to count more without letting a word repeated in both fields dominate. Which approach fits BM25F's reasoning?
options: Score each field with BM25 and sum, with title boost 2
Set k1 = 0 on both fields
Set b = 1 on the description so long descriptions are ignored
Pool weighted counts across fields, then saturate once, for example with combined_fields
explain: Summing per-field scores saturates each field separately, so the same word repeated across fields keeps adding nearly full weight. BM25F pools the evidence for a term first, then applies one saturation, while field weights still let the title count more.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Training it: initialization, AdamW and a warmup plus cosine schedule
question: Which parameters does nanoGPT's configure_optimizers exclude from weight decay?
options: The token embedding table, because it is tied
All attention weights
Nothing; AdamW decays every tensor equally
Tensors with fewer than 2 dimensions: biases and LayerNorm weights
explain: The rule is p.dim() >= 2 gets weight_decay, everything else gets 0. So matmul weights and embeddings (including the tied wte) are decayed, while 1-D biases and LayerNorm gains and shifts are not.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Generating text: the sampling loop, temperature, top-k and top-p
question: Why does generate keep only `logits[:, -1, :]`?
options: Earlier positions' logits are always wrong
It saves memory and gives the same result as averaging all positions
Only the last position's logits predict the token that comes after the current context
The causal mask zeroes out the other positions' logits
explain: Position t's logits predict token t+1. Earlier positions predict tokens that already exist in the context, so they are useless here. The causal mask zeroes attention weights, not logits.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Many inputs: partial derivatives and the gradient vector
question: At some point the gradient of a loss is $(0, 0)$. What can you conclude?
options: It is the global minimum
It is a local minimum
It is a critical point (for example a minimum, a maximum, or a saddle); the gradient alone cannot tell which
The loss must be constant everywhere
explain: A local minimum is lower than every nearby point; the global minimum is the lowest point anywhere. A zero gradient only says that no direction has a slope, as measured by first derivatives. Points like that are called critical points. $x^2 - y^2$ at the origin has zero gradient but is a saddle: it rises along $x$ and falls along $y$. Lesson 7 shows how second derivatives tell these apart.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Jacobians: derivatives of vector-valued functions
question: Three layers have Jacobians $J_3 J_2 J_1$, each $1000 \times 1000$, and the loss gradient is a $1 \times 1000$ row $g$. Which evaluation order of $g J_3 J_2 J_1$ is cheapest?
options: Compute $J_3 J_2 J_1$ first, then multiply by $g$
Any order; matrix multiplication gives the same cost
Left to right: $((g J_3) J_2) J_1$, so every step is a row times a matrix
Right to left, starting from $J_1$
explain: Left to right keeps a single row: three row-matrix products of about $10^6$ multiplications each. Multiplying two $1000 \times 1000$ matrices takes about $10^9$. The result is the same in any order, but the cost is not. This left-to-right order is reverse mode, the subject of the next lesson.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Writing scripts: arguments, tests, if, loops and functions
question: With `name="Ana Lee"`, a script runs `if [ $name = admin ]; then echo yes; else echo no; fi`. What is printed?
options: no, because the strings differ
yes, because `[` compares only the first word
an error from `[` (too many arguments), then no
nothing, because bash refuses to run the if
explain: Unquoted, `$name` splits into Ana and Lee, so `[` receives `Ana Lee = admin ]`, which is not a valid expression. It prints `[: too many arguments` and returns 2, and any non-zero status sends if to the else branch (real bash run). Quoting gives `[ "Ana Lee" = admin ]`, a clean false.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Exit statuses and scripts that fail loudly
question: A script has `set -e`. Its line `grep -q TODO notes.txt && echo found` runs when notes.txt has no TODO. What happens?
options: The script exits with status 1 because grep failed
Nothing prints and the script continues with the next line
The script exits with status 127
The echo runs because && ignores failures under -e
explain: grep is not the final command of the `&&` list, so its failure is exempt from -e. The echo is skipped and execution continues. (If this were the last line, the script's own exit status would still be 1.)

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Learning word vectors by predicting their neighbours
question: Two words, *Paris* and *Rome*, never appear in the same sentence in the training corpus. Can skip-gram still give them similar vectors?
options: No, they must co-occur to be pulled together
Yes, if they share many context words such as city, capital and visited
Only if they are in the same window at least once
Only with CBOW, not skip-gram
explain: Similarity comes from shared contexts, not direct co-occurrence. Both input vectors are trained to score highly against the same output vectors (u_city, u_capital, ...), which pushes them toward the same region of the space.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Evaluating and visualizing an embedding space
question: Model A scores 0.33 on WordSim-353 and 0.20 on SimLex-999. Model B scores 0.30 and 0.35. You need a thesaurus that must never list antonyms as synonyms. Which evidence matters more?
options: WordSim-353, because it is older and more widely reported
The sum of both scores
SimLex-999, because it rates antonyms as dissimilar, which is exactly your requirement: prefer model B
Neither: only analogy accuracy measures synonymy
explain: SimLex-999 rewards models that separate similarity from association, which is what a thesaurus needs. WordSim-353 asked raters to treat antonyms as similar, so a high score there can come from placing antonyms close.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Contrastive training in practice: in-batch negatives and collapse
question: You train a contrastive image model with $\tau = 1$ and unnormalized dot products. The contrastive loss falls nicely, but a linear classifier trained on the representation scores poorly. Which change does SimCLR's ablation most directly support?
options: Remove the negatives so the model only sees positives
Increase tau to 10 to smooth the loss
Take the representation from z instead of h
Use cosine similarity (l2 normalization) with a tuned, smaller temperature
explain: SimCLR reports that without l2 normalization the contrastive task gets easier but the representation is worse under linear evaluation, and that a proper temperature matters too. Removing negatives invites collapse (everything maps to one point), a larger tau flattens the softmax further, and h, not z, is the better representation.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Prefill and decode: FLOPs and bytes per generated token
question: Which change most reduces time to first token for a request with a very long prompt?
options: Faster HBM only
More math throughput (or splitting prefill across GPUs), since prefill is compute-bound
A larger decode batch
Lowering the number of output tokens
explain: TTFT is dominated by prefill (plus any queueing), and prefill of many tokens is compute-bound. Output length affects total latency, not TTFT.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Measure it: tokens per second, MBU and MFU
question: Batch-1 decode of a 7B FP16 model on an A100 measures 35% MBU. Which pair of causes is most likely?
options: The KV cache is too small, and the prompt is too short
Tensor Cores are too slow, and the clock is too high
Per-kernel launch overhead from eager Python code, and elementwise work not fused into the matmul kernels
Too many warps per SM, and too much L2 cache
explain: At batch 1 each kernel is tiny, so the time between kernels (Python, launches) is a large share of each step; gpt-fast went from about 17% to about 70% of the 6.57 ms floor by removing it (the post reports 72% MBU using a rounder 2 TB/s). Unfused extra kernels add reads and launches too. Math speed is irrelevant to a memory-bound step.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Where a program's memory lives: code, heap and stack
question: Why does sumsq copy b into rbx before calling square, instead of leaving it in rsi?
options: Because rsi is reserved for return values
Because square may overwrite rsi freely, while the ABI requires square to preserve rbx
Because rbx is faster than rsi
Because the stack is full
explain: The System V ABI splits registers into caller-saved ones (like rdi, rsi, rax) that any callee may clobber, and callee-saved ones (rbx, rbp, r12 to r15) that a callee must restore before returning. That is also why sumsq itself pushes rbx and r14 first: it is about to use them and must hand them back intact.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Virtual memory: every process gets its own addresses
question: With 4 KiB pages, what is the offset within its page of virtual address 0x7ffd12345678?
explain: 4 KiB = 2^12 bytes, so the offset is the low 12 bits, which is the last 3 hex digits: 0x678. The remaining bits select the page through the 4-level table.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Supervised fine-tuning: same loss, curated data, masked prompt
question: A team fine-tunes on chat data but forgets to mask the prompt. What is the most likely symptom?
options: Training crashes because labels and logits have different lengths
The model learns to write user-style questions and the loss is dominated by hard-to-predict prompt tokens
The model forgets the chat template entirely
Nothing changes, because the prompt loss gradient is always zero
explain: Without the mask the model is also trained to predict user text, which is high-entropy and dominates the average (78 percent of the summed loss in our example). Capacity and gradient go into imitating users instead of answering them.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: RL with PPO: maximize reward, stay close to the SFT model
question: Why does InstructGPT keep a frozen copy of the SFT model during RL?
options: To generate the training prompts
To compute log-probabilities for the KL penalty that anchors the policy
To replace the reward model when it is uncertain
To serve as the value function
explain: The frozen SFT model supplies log pi_SFT for every sampled token, which the per-token KL penalty compares with the policy's log-probabilities. The value function is a separate model initialized from the reward model.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Answering AND queries by merging postings
question: You intersect a 10-entry list with a 1,000,000-entry list using the plain two-pointer merge. Roughly how many steps can it take in the worst case?
options: About 10, because the result has at most 10 documents
About 20, because each short entry costs two comparisons
About 1,000,000, because the pointer may have to walk the long list nearly to its end
About log2(1,000,000) = 20 per entry, because the lists are sorted
explain: The plain merge advances one step at a time, so in the worst case it walks the whole long list: O(x + y). Doing about 20 steps per short entry is what you get only if you add skips or binary search into the long list, which the plain merge does not do.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: C in one sitting: types, operators, control flow and functions
question: `int a = -7, b = 2;` What are `a / b` and `a % b` in C99 and later?
options: -4 and 1
-3 and 1
-3 and -1
explain: Both operands are int, so this is integer division, which truncates toward zero: -3.5 becomes -3, not -4. The remainder must satisfy (a/b)*b + a%b == a, that is -6 + a%b == -7, so a%b is -1. The remainder takes the sign of the left operand.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Arrays, pointer arithmetic and strings
question: A function `void clear(char *buf)` does `memset(buf, 0, sizeof buf);` (memset sets that many bytes to 0) and callers pass a `char buf[256]`. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, sizeof buf is 256
It clears only 8 bytes, because buf is a pointer inside the function
It clears 257 bytes including the terminator
It fails to compile because arrays cannot be passed
explain: Inside clear, buf is a char *, so sizeof buf is the pointer size (8 on 64-bit platforms), not 256. The array's size is lost at the call. The fix is `void clear(char *buf, size_t n)` and `memset(buf, 0, n)`.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Function pointers and void *: writing generic code like qsort
question: `const char *w[] = {"pear", "fig", "kiwi"};` is sorted with `qsort(w, 3, sizeof w[0], cmp)`. Which cmp is correct?
options: return strcmp(a, b);
return strcmp(*(const char * const *)a, *(const char * const *)b);
return strcmp((const char *)a, (const char *)b);
return *(const char *)a - *(const char *)b;
explain: Each element of w is a `const char *`, so qsort passes a pointer to one: a `const char * const *`. Dereferencing it gives the string. Options 1 and 3 treat the address of the pointer as if it were the characters. Option 4 compares the first bytes of the pointers themselves, not the strings. A test sort with option 2 gave fig kiwi pear.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Debugging C: gdb and Valgrind on a real crash
question: A third-party library, shipped only as a compiled binary, seems to corrupt the heap in your Linux service. You cannot recompile it. Which tool fits first?
options: AddressSanitizer, by adding -fsanitize=address to your own build
Valgrind memcheck on the existing binary
-Wall -Wextra on your own code
gdb with a breakpoint on main
explain: Valgrind instruments the program at run time, including code in libraries you did not compile, so no rebuild is needed. ASan only instruments code compiled with the flag, and warnings only see your source. A debugger helps once you know where to look.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Borrowing: many readers or one writer
question: A colleague says the Vec error is pointless in single-threaded code because no other thread can touch `v`. What is the best reply?
options: They are right; the check only matters with threads
`push` may reallocate and free the old buffer, so `first` could dangle even with one thread
`push` always copies the vector, so `first` becomes stale but still safe to read
explain: Reallocation frees the old block, so the shared reference could point at freed memory: a use after free with no threads involved. `push` only reallocates when length equals capacity, which is exactly why the danger is easy to miss in testing.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Structs that borrow: lifetimes in types and what 'static means
question: A struct holds a borrowed field: `struct Parser<'a> { input: &'a str }`. What does the `'a` promise?
options: The `Parser` lives for the whole program
The `input` string is copied into the `Parser`
A `Parser` value cannot outlive the string data that `input` borrows
The `Parser` owns the string and will drop it
explain: A lifetime parameter on a struct ties the struct's validity to the borrowed data. The struct does not own the string, and nothing is copied. The checker rejects any use of the `Parser` after the borrowed string is dropped.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: The dot product: one number that measures alignment
question: A search system ranks documents by raw dot product with the query embedding. Users complain that long, rambling documents always win. Which change most directly targets the cause?
options: Use more embedding dimensions
Square every dot product before ranking
Add a constant to every component of the query
Rank by cosine similarity, or normalize all embeddings to unit length
explain: If document vectors grow longer with document length, the dot product rewards that length. Dividing by the norms (cosine) keeps only direction. More dimensions or squaring the score keeps the length effect; adding a constant changes the query's direction, not the bias.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Determinant and inverse: undoing a map and solving Ax = b
question: $\det A = 3$ and $\det B = -2$ for two $2 \times 2$ matrices. What is $\det(AB)$, and is $AB$ invertible?
options: -6, and AB is invertible
1, and AB is invertible
-6, and AB is not invertible because its determinant is negative
6, and AB is invertible
explain: Determinants multiply under composition: $3 \times (-2) = -6$. Any nonzero determinant means no direction is squashed flat, so $AB$ has an inverse, $B^{-1}A^{-1}$. The sign only records the orientation flip that $B$ introduces.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Where it shows up: linear layers, batches and attention scores
question: A colleague removes the $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ factor and raises $d_k$ from 64 to 1024. What do you expect?
options: Nothing changes, because softmax only depends on the ranking of scores
Scores shrink toward 0, so attention becomes uniform
Scores spread about 4 times wider, softmax gets much peakier and training can slow because gradients shrink
The product QK^T becomes undefined
explain: Typical score size grows like $\sqrt{d_k}$: $\sqrt{1024}/\sqrt{64} = 4$. Softmax depends on score *differences*, not just their ranking, so wider scores mean near one-hot weights and tiny gradients. Shapes still match, so nothing errors.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Classification end to end: logistic regression, boundaries and softmax
question: A softmax classifier gives probabilities (0.7, 0.2, 0.1) and the correct class is the third. What is the gradient of the loss with respect to the three scores?
explain: The gradient is $p$ minus the one-hot label (0, 0, 1): $(0.7, 0.2, 0.1 - 1) = (0.7, 0.2, -0.9)$. Gradient descent subtracts it, so the wrong classes' scores go down and the correct one goes up, most strongly where the model was most wrong.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Measuring a model: metrics, thresholds and cross-validation
question: A disease screen is positive for 50 of 10,000 patients. Model A has AUC 0.97; at its chosen threshold it flags 500 patients, 45 of them sick. What are its precision and recall?
options: Precision 0.97, recall 0.97
Precision 0.09, recall 0.90
Precision 0.90, recall 0.09
Precision 0.45, recall 0.90
explain: Precision = 45/500 = 0.09: 91 percent of flags are false alarms. Recall = 45/50 = 0.90. A high AUC says the model ranks well, not that its flags are mostly right when positives are this rare.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Why a single linear layer cannot learn XOR
question: A network has three hidden layers of 512 units each, but every activation is the identity. Which statement is true?
options: It can only represent affine functions of its input, same as a single linear layer
It can represent any continuous function given enough units
It can represent XOR but not more complex functions
It is equivalent to a single hidden layer network with ReLU
explain: Each layer is affine and the composition of affine maps is affine, so the whole stack collapses to $W'x+b'$. The extra parameters add cost but no expressive power.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Backpropagation through a whole network, by hand
question: A colleague implements BP2 as `d1 = (W2 @ d2) * a1 * (1 - a1)` for a network where W2 has shape (10, 64). What happens?
options: It works, matrix order does not matter
It computes the gradient for the biases instead
It fails or computes garbage: the error must go back through the transpose, W2.T @ d2, giving one value per hidden unit
It only breaks when the batch size is 1
explain: W2 maps 64 hidden units to 10 outputs. Going backward, the 10 output errors must be distributed to 64 hidden units along the same connections: that is $(W^2)^\top \delta^2$, shape 64. W2 @ d2 is a shape error here, and for square matrices it silently produces wrong gradients, which a gradient check would catch.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Training a real network: an MLP on handwritten digits
question: You train a 10-class classifier and the very first loss printed is 9.7. What does that most likely tell you?
options: Training is going well; high loss means room to improve
The initial logits are far from uniform (for example, weights initialised too large), or the loss is computed wrongly
The dataset has more than 10 classes
The learning rate is too small
explain: With small random weights the logits are nearly equal and the loss should be about $\ln 10 = 2.30$. A much larger value means the network starts out confidently wrong, typically from oversized initial weights, or there is a bug such as applying the loss to the wrong tensor. Check this before training.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Virtual memory: paging, page tables and the TLB
question: In the same 16 KB example, a program touches virtual page 100 (binary 0110 0100). What happens?
options: The hardware reads the PTE at index 4 of the page at frame 100
The PDE at index 6 is invalid, so the hardware raises an exception without reading any page of PTEs
The MMU allocates a new page of PTEs for that region
It maps to frame 100, the first valid entry
explain: The directory index is the top 4 bits, 0110 = 6, and only PDEs 0 and 15 are valid. An invalid PDE means no PTE in that 16-page region is valid, so the access traps right away. Allocating page-table pages is the OS's job, not the MMU's.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Concurrency bugs: atomicity, ordering and deadlock
question: A team makes every thread acquire locks in increasing address order. Which deadlock condition does that remove?
options: Mutual exclusion
Hold-and-wait
No preemption
Circular wait
explain: Threads still hold locks exclusively, still hold one while waiting for the next, and locks still cannot be taken away. But a cycle would need some thread to hold a higher lock while waiting for a lower one, which the order forbids, so circular wait cannot form.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Crash consistency: fsck and journaling
question: A crash leaves only the new inode I[v2] on disk; the bitmap B[v2] and data block Db were not written. What is the state?
options: Inconsistent: the inode points to a block the bitmap says is free, and that block holds old garbage
Consistent and correct: the inode is the source of truth
A harmless space leak
Lost data but a consistent file system
explain: The inode now points to the new data block (block 5 in OSTEP), but Db never reached it, so reading the file returns whatever was there before. The bitmap still says that block is free, contradicting the inode. This is the case fsck or journaling exists to prevent. Only-Db is the harmless case; only-bitmap is the leak.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Joint and marginal distributions, and the chain rule of probability
question: Using the spam table (0.24, 0.06, 0.07, 0.63), what is P(contains free | not spam)?
options: 0.07, the joint cell
0.31, the share of all emails containing free
0.23, which is 70 of the 310 emails containing free
0.10, which is 70 of the 700 non-spam emails
explain: Condition on not spam: take that row (0.07 and 0.63, total 0.70) and divide: 0.07 / 0.70 = 0.10. Option C divides by the wrong total: it is P(not spam | free), the reversed conditional.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Covariance, correlation and the multivariate Gaussian
question: Two features in your data have correlation 0. What can you safely conclude?
options: They are independent, so a model gains nothing from using both
They have no linear association, but one may still depend strongly on the other
Their covariance matrix is the identity
One of them is constant
explain: Zero correlation rules out a linear trend only; y = x squared on symmetric x has correlation 0 and full dependence. The covariance matrix is diagonal, but not the identity unless both variances are 1.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Confidence intervals, p-values and an A/B test
question: Two experiments find the same 0.2 point lift in conversion. Experiment 1 (50,000 users) has p = 0.01; experiment 2 (5,000 users) has p = 0.40. What is the best conclusion?
options: Experiment 2 shows the lift is absent
The experiments contradict each other
Both are consistent with the same lift; experiment 2 is too small to distinguish it from noise
Experiment 1 must have a bug, since the lifts match but p differs
explain: Same effect, ten times fewer users means a standard error about sqrt(10) = 3.2 times larger, so a much smaller z and larger p. A non-significant result is not evidence of no effect; its confidence interval is just wide enough to include 0.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Fixed budget, best split: IsoFLOP curves
question: On an IsoFLOP curve, why does loss rise again for the largest models at a fixed budget?
options: Large models overfit any dataset
With compute fixed, a larger N leaves fewer tokens, so the data term B/D^beta grows
Large models have a larger irreducible loss E
Backward passes cost more than forward passes
explain: At fixed C, $D = C/(6N)$. Pushing N up shrinks D, and the finite-data penalty grows faster than the finite-model penalty falls. E is the same for every model, and the 6N cost is already accounted for in the budget.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Batch size, learning rate and data limits as you scale
question: You have 300B unique tokens and compute for 3T tokens of training (10 epochs). Which plan does data-constrained scaling favour?
options: Repeat the data on a model somewhat smaller than the fresh-data optimum, accepting that later epochs are worth less
Train once on 300B tokens and leave 90 percent of the compute unused, since repeated data is worthless
Train a 10x larger model on one epoch, since extra parameters keep their full value
Use the fresh-data optimal model for 3T tokens, since repeats are exactly as good as fresh data
explain: At 10 epochs $D' \approx 7.8\,U_D$: repeats still add a lot, but less than fresh data would. Excess parameters decay faster than repeated data ($R_N^{*} \approx 5.3$ against $R_D^{*} \approx 15.4$), so the optimum shifts toward a smaller model on more epochs. Repeats are not worthless before roughly 40 epochs.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Graded relevance and nDCG: rewarding the best result first
question: Two teams score the same run on the same qrels and report nDCG@10 of 0.576 and 0.523. Neither has a bug. What is the most likely explanation?
options: One used a natural log instead of log base 2 in the discount
One used linear gain g and the other exponential gain 2^g - 1
One computed nDCG@5 by mistake
nDCG is randomized, so small differences are expected
explain: These are exactly q1's values under the two gain conventions. Changing the log base alone would not change nDCG at all, since the same constant factor appears in DCG and IDCG and cancels. nDCG@5 is 0.411 here, and nDCG is deterministic.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Searching a corpus: indexing, ANN and vector size
question: With an E5 model, queries are embedded with the `query: ` prefix, but the corpus was indexed last year with no prefix at all. What should you expect?
options: Weaker retrieval, because passages were embedded without the passage prefix the model expects
No effect: the prefix only matters at training time
An error, because the vectors have different dimensions
Better retrieval, because mixing conventions adds diversity
explain: The model card instructs that each input start with query: or passage:, and the model was trained that way. The vectors still have the same dimension, so nothing crashes; quality degrades silently. Re-embed the corpus with the right prefix.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Encoding new text: replay the merges in rank order
question: A teammate's encoder, given lowest, first merges (l, o) because l o is the leftmost pair present in the merge list. Is the final result different here, and what is the bug?
options: Different result; the merge list should be applied left to right
Same result here, but the rule is wrong: merges must be applied by lowest rank, and on other inputs left to right gives splits the model never saw
Same result, and the rule is fine since merges commute
Different result; BPE merges the most frequent pair in the current word
explain: For lowest both orders happen to end at low est_. But BPE's contract is rank order: the encoder must reproduce the segmentation used during training. Merges do not commute in general (merging one pair can destroy an overlapping one), so a left-to-right encoder can disagree with the model's training data on other inputs.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Tradeoffs: vocab size, numbers, languages, glitch tokens, alternatives
question: A team moves a code assistant from the GPT-2 tokenizer to cl100k_base. On their Python files bytes per token goes from about 2 to about 4. Which effect should they expect, with the model's context window unchanged in tokens?
options: No change, because the text is the same number of bytes
Each file costs fewer tokens, and the embedding table also shrinks because tokens are longer
Each file costs more tokens, because a bigger vocabulary means longer ids
About twice as much code fits in the same context, and each file needs about half as many positions to process; the cost is a vocabulary about twice as large
explain: Doubling bytes per token halves the tokens for the same bytes, so about twice as much code fits in the window and about half as many positions are processed. The table does not shrink: it has one row per vocabulary entry, so it grows from 50,257 to about 100k rows, in the embedding and in the output layer.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Optimizers: momentum, Adam and decoupled weight decay
question: You switch from `torch.optim.Adam(params, lr=1e-3, weight_decay=0.01)` to `torch.optim.AdamW(params, lr=1e-3, weight_decay=0.01)`. What changes?
options: Nothing; the two classes are aliases
Decay is now applied directly as w -= lr x 0.01 x w, instead of being added to the gradient and rescaled by 1/sqrt(v)
AdamW disables bias correction
AdamW applies decay only to biases
explain: Adam's weight_decay adds lambda x w to the gradient, which then passes through the m/sqrt(v) ratio. AdamW shrinks the weights in a separate step, so every weight decays at the rate lr x lambda regardless of its gradient history.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: BatchNorm, LayerNorm, RMSNorm and dropout: train vs eval mode
question: You train a model whose batches have only 2 examples per GPU and see unstable results. Which normalization is the natural fix?
options: BatchNorm with momentum 0.01
LayerNorm, since its statistics come from each example alone
Increase dropout to 0.9
Remove the learned gamma and beta
explain: Batch statistics from 2 examples are extremely noisy. LayerNorm's mean and variance are computed over one example's features, so batch size does not matter. The LayerNorm paper names batch-size dependence as the limitation it was designed to remove.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: Why exact nearest-neighbor search stops scaling
question: Your collection grows from 1 million to 4 million vectors and you upgrade to a machine with 2x the memory bandwidth. Under the linear-scan model, what happens to brute-force latency?
options: It doubles: 4x the data over 2x the bandwidth
It stays the same, because the bandwidth doubled
It quadruples, because bandwidth does not affect latency
It halves, because more bandwidth beats more data
explain: Brute force reads every vector, so time scales with N divided by bandwidth: 4 / 2 = 2x slower. Hardware gives constant factors; the linear growth in N remains.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: Tuning ef and M, and choosing between HNSW, IVF and PQ
question: A query with a selective filter (1 percent of rows match) returns 0 or 1 results from an HNSW index with ef_search = 40. Which explanation fits?
options: The graph is disconnected, so the filtered rows are unreachable
The index post-filters about 40 candidates, so about 0.4 match on average
Cosine distance cannot be combined with WHERE clauses
ef_search is ignored when a filter is present
explain: With post-filtering, expected matches = candidates times selectivity = 40 x 0.01 = 0.4. Raise ef_search, enable iterative scans, or use a separate index or partition for that filter.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Typosquatting and dependency confusion: winning by name
question: A team uses `pip install --extra-index-url <private>` and their internal package is version 3.2.0. An attacker publishes the same name on PyPI as 3.1.9. What does pip install?
options: Both versions side by side
Nothing; pip errors on duplicate names
3.1.9, because PyPI is the main index
3.2.0, because it is the best match across all indexes
explain: No index has priority and the highest matching version wins, so here the private 3.2.0 wins. The attack only works when the attacker picks a higher number, which is why Birsan used high versions. The design flaw remains: whoever publishes the highest number decides.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: CI secrets: Codecov and the keys inside every pipeline
question: A pipeline needs to publish a package. Which setup leaves the least for a Codecov-style script to steal?
options: The token hard-coded in the workflow file
The token only in the publish job, as an environment variable
OIDC trusted publishing in a dedicated publish job that runs no third-party tools
A long-lived registry token stored as a repository secret, available to all jobs
explain: With OIDC there is no stored token at all; the short-lived credential is minted for that job and expires. Isolating the publish job keeps third-party code away from it.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: SBOMs: an ingredients list you can query when the alarm rings
question: Which question can an SBOM answer on its own?
options: Is any component in this product malicious?
Which of our products contain ms version 2.1.3, and through which dependency path?
Is the vulnerable function actually called?
Was the build server compromised?
explain: Inventory and relationships are exactly what an SBOM records. Maliciousness, build integrity and reachability need other data: advisories, provenance and code analysis.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: When a dependency is compromised: a response playbook
question: A developer's laptop installed axios 1.14.1 at 01:10 UTC on 31 March 2026. They have since upgraded to 1.15.0. What is the correct next step?
options: Run npm audit and close the ticket if it is clean
Delete node_modules and reinstall
Treat the laptop as compromised: rotate every credential it held from another machine, investigate it, and rebuild it
Nothing: the upgrade removed the malicious code
explain: The postinstall dropper installed a separate remote access trojan and erased its traces. The axios post-mortem says to treat the machine as compromised and rotate every secret, token and credential on it.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Replace versus accumulate: what keeps the error bounded
question: Under accumulation with d = 10, T = 100 and noise variance 1, what is the test error after iteration 2?
options: 0.225, twice the first iteration
0.112, unchanged
0.185, the bound
0.140, which is 1.25 times the first iteration
explain: The sum is 1 + 1/4 = 1.25, so the error is 0.1124 x 1.25 = 0.140. Doubling (0.225) is the replace result.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: What happens when your program calls write
question: Why does the x86-64 Linux syscall convention pass the 4th argument in r10 instead of rcx, which the normal C calling convention uses?
options: The syscall instruction overwrites rcx with the user return address
The kernel needs rcx to hold the syscall number
r10 is faster to read from kernel mode
rcx is reserved for the error code
explain: The `syscall` instruction saves the return address in rcx and rflags in r11, so anything you put in rcx is destroyed by the instruction itself. The kernel's entry comment notes that arg3 arrives in r10 and must be moved to rcx to match the C ABI before calling C handlers.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: MAP_SHARED, MAP_PRIVATE and copy-on-write
question: Two worker processes map the same data file. Worker 1 uses MAP_SHARED and writes a record. Worker 2 uses MAP_PRIVATE and has only read that page. Which statement is guaranteed?
options: Worker 2 sees the new record immediately
Worker 2 never sees the new record
Whether worker 2 sees it is unspecified, so code must not depend on it
The write fails because a private mapping of the page exists
explain: mmap(2) states it is unspecified whether changes made to the file after the mmap call are visible in a MAP_PRIVATE mapping. In practice an untouched private page often still points at the page cache page, but once worker 2 writes that page it has its own copy. Use MAP_SHARED in both if they must see each other's writes.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Fan-out: why one server's p99 becomes everyone's problem
question: Why does fan-out make tail latency matter more than median latency for the user?
options: Because the root averages the leaf latencies, and averages are dominated by outliers
Because leaves process requests serially
Because the user waits for the slowest of N responses, so a rare per-leaf event becomes a common per-request event
Because median latency cannot be measured at the root
explain: The root waits for the maximum, not the mean, of the leaf latencies. The probability that the maximum includes a tail event grows as 1 - (1-p)^N.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: How a mobile network fits together: radio, core and the HLR
question: A partner network sends your HLR a request about IMSI 234150999999999. Your network is MCC 234, MNC 15. What does the IMSI tell your HLR?
options: Nothing: an IMSI is just a random serial number
Which country the subscriber is in right now
That the subscriber is yours, because the MCC and MNC name your network as home
The subscriber's phone number
explain: The MCC and MNC at the start of an IMSI identify the home network (TS 23.003). They say nothing about where the phone is now (that is the HLR's location record), and the phone number is the separate MSISDN.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: Diameter in 4G roaming: the same trust model on IP
question: Why is checking Origin-Realm alone not enough?
options: Origin-Realm is encrypted and cannot be read
Origin-Realm only exists in SS7
Realms change every hour
Origin-Realm is written by the sender, so it must be bound to the authenticated peer or connection the message actually came from
explain: The field is a claim. Without binding it to the transport peer, a rogue sender with interconnect access simply writes a partner's realm. 5G makes this binding explicit at the SEPP.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: SIM and eSIM: the key in your pocket, and how it gets there
question: Why could Simjacker work on phones from almost every manufacturer?
options: All those phones ran the same operating system version
It exploited a bug in the radio chipset of every phone
It used SS7 to change each phone's firmware
The vulnerable software was the S@T Browser on the SIM card, and phones passed the SMS to the card
explain: CERT-EU notes the attack depends on software on the UICC, not the device. Handsets forward such messages to the card, so the brand of phone did not matter; that is also why the fix sat with operators and card settings.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: Satellite links: segments, footprints and cleartext GEO traffic
question: Why can one receiving station observe traffic meant for terminals hundreds of kilometres away?
options: A GEO transponder's forward link is broadcast across a footprint that can cover a third of Earth, so any dish inside it can receive the signal
Satellites forward every packet to every country on purpose
The researchers hacked the satellites
Terminals send copies of their traffic to anyone who asks
explain: The study was passive: it received broadcasts. GEO footprints are huge by design, which is why confidentiality has to come from encryption, not from location.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a telecom and space defence map
question: Which pair of controls addresses the same underlying problem in two generations of signalling?
options: SMS home routing and Galileo OSNMA
SUCI and router golden configs
Satellite IPsec and carrier account locks
SS7 category 2 filtering and the 5G SEPP's check of the originating network ID against the peer's certificate
explain: Both decide whether the sender may speak about this subscriber or network. Category 2 filtering compares the sender's GT with the IMSI's home; the SEPP compares the claimed network ID with what the authenticated peer's certificate represents, which closes the spoofing gap.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Allen relations, current roles and time-scoped queries
question: Which pair of toy roles is in the relation *finishes*?
options: B finishes A
C finishes D
E finishes D
A finishes C
explain: E (Mar 2024 to Present) and D (Sep 2021 to Present) end at the same point and E starts later, so E finishes D. B is during A, A is before C, and C overlaps or precedes D depending on the convention.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Verifiers set the ceiling: error rates, GenRM and self-verification
question: A verifier has true positive rate 0.95 and false positive rate 0.02. On a problem where 2% of samples are correct, what accuracy does best-of-N approach as N grows?
options: About 0.95, its true positive rate
About 0.98, one minus its false positive rate
About 1.0, because coverage reaches 1
About 0.49
explain: The ceiling is $pt / (pt + (1-p)f) = 0.019 / (0.019 + 0.0196) = 0.49$. Correct accepted samples and wrong accepted samples arrive at almost the same rate because wrong samples outnumber correct ones 49 to 1.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Exchanging test-time compute for a bigger model
question: Using Snell et al.'s FLOPs model with M = 14, how much more inference compute can the small model use at R = 1?

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: One gradient step on a key-value loss is the delta rule
question: Which pair of choices turns the generic TTT layer into plain linear attention?
options: Linear model, batch gradient descent, W_0 = 0
Linear model, online gradient descent, W_0 = 0
Two-layer MLP, batch gradient descent, learned W_0
Nadaraya-Watson kernel regression with a softmax kernel
explain: Theorem 1 of the TTT paper: linear model, batch GD (all gradients at W_0) and W_0 = 0 give linear attention. Online GD gives the delta rule instead. The kernel-regression option is Theorem 2, which recovers softmax attention, not linear attention. Nadaraya-Watson kernel regression predicts a weighted average of stored values, weighted by a kernel's similarity between the query and each stored key.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Titans' three architectures, worked one segment at a time
question: In Titans (MAC) at test time, which part keeps changing its weights as the input streams in?
options: The persistent memory tokens
The attention projections W_Q, W_K, W_V
All three, since Titans fine-tunes itself at test time
The neural long-term memory M
explain: The paper is explicit: persistent memory parameters stay fixed because they encode task knowledge, the attention weights are fixed in-context learners, and only the long-term memory keeps learning (memorizing) at test time.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: One lock, many cores: why a shared slab cache stops scaling
question: Why did the original slab allocator get *slower* in total when going from 1 to 16 threads, rather than just staying flat?
options: Each thread ran its constructors twice
Contention made each lock handoff more expensive (cache line transfers, waiting, wakeups), so the serialized work itself took longer
The Starfire had only one memory controller
The slab layer disabled interrupts
explain: A flat ceiling assumes the critical section costs the same under load. Under contention the lock and freelist lines move between CPUs on every acquisition and waiters spin or sleep, so each serialized operation gets slower. The paper calls this increasingly pathological lock contention.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: Today: thread caches, per-CPU caches and restartable sequences
question: In TCMalloc's rseq push (free), the code writes the object pointer into the slot and then stores the incremented `current`. Why is it fine if the thread is preempted between those two stores?
options: Preemption is disabled during free
The slot write is atomic
Nothing is published until the store to current commits; a restarted sequence just overwrites the same slot
The kernel replays the first store for it
explain: Only the final store to `current` makes the new object visible. If the thread is interrupted after writing the slot but before committing, the sequence restarts, recomputes the slot from the current header and rewrites it. TCMalloc's rseq notes describe exactly this: preempted sequences overwrite the deallocated object until one commits.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: Stacking: let the rare thing rise to the top
question: Stacking scheduled task names across all machines gives 4,800 values that each appear once. What most likely went wrong?
options: The query needs a longer time range
Stacking does not work on scheduled tasks
The key contains a variable part (for example a user name or GUID) that should be normalised first
The fleet is heavily compromised
explain: A long tail made of thousands of singletons usually means the values differ only in an irrelevant part. Replace the variable part with a placeholder and stack again; the real outliers then stand out from a short tail.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: Hunting in network data: rare, regular and unresolved
question: Host A's connection gaps to one address have a mean of 300 seconds and a standard deviation of 3 seconds. Host B's have a mean of 300 and a standard deviation of 240. Which is more likely automated check-ins, and what is each CV?
options: A: CV 0.01; B: CV 0.8. A is machine-like
Both are identical because the means are equal
B: CV 0.8 is more regular than A
explain: CV = standard deviation / mean: 3 / 300 = 0.01 for A and 240 / 300 = 0.8 for B. A connects almost exactly every five minutes, which is how scheduled software (benign or malicious) behaves. B varies like human activity. Next step for A: which process makes the connection, and is the destination rare?

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: Measuring a hunt programme, and where to practise
question: A hunt is disproven: no ntds.dit copies on any domain controller in 90 days. What belongs in its write-up?
options: A statement that the network is secure
The hypothesis, data and time range checked, queries used, known-benign ntdsutil uses by named admins, any gaps found, and the detection or baseline it produced
Only the queries
Nothing; disproven hunts are not documented
